main_damage_causes: Ginny's expressive, excitable personality is flattened to a single generic line, eliminating the first impression the books carefully construct
Her emotional star-struck reaction to Harry — the seed of their relationship — is cut entirely, removing early relational groundwork
Her vivid physical action (running after the train, half-laughing half-crying) that establishes her as emotionally present and memorable is absent, making her effectively invisible in her debut scene

Removal of Ginny's near-confession (Book Scenes 91-104) eliminates her moral agency and active resistance to Riddle's control, reducing her from a character fighting her own victimhood to a purely passive plot device.

Systematic omission of counterbalancing characterisation (her normal volubility, her wit, her recovery on the train) leaves the film with only the one-dimensional shy/terrified/weeping version of Ginny, with no evidence of the confident, humorous person she actually is.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – King's Cross, Ginny's only line is 'Good luck'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Ginny as excitable, emotionally expressive, and already star-struck by Harry: she squeals 'Harry Potter!', points at him, begs to go on the train, runs alongside it crying and laughing, and waves until it disappears. She is a vivid, energetic presence who makes a clear impression.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny's entire role at King's Cross is reduced to a single two-word line: 'Good luck.' She has no reaction to Harry, no excitement, no emotional farewell to her brothers, no running after the train. She is essentially a silent background figure.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this scene to establish Ginny's personality — her enthusiasm, her crush on Harry, her warmth — before she even properly enters the story. The film collapses all of that into a generic pleasantry, giving the audience no impression of who she is.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – King's Cross, Ginny's star-struck reaction to Harry is absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 13–15 (Chamber of Secrets platform) reinforces a pattern established in Book Scenes 4–12: Ginny singles Harry out by name, squeals, and points at him, showing she already has a specific emotional relationship to Harry before he knows her well. This foreshadows and seeds their eventual romantic arc.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny shows no recognition of or reaction to Harry at King's Cross. The seeding of her feelings for Harry — a defining trait in this portion of the book corpus — is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Ginny's one-sided awareness of Harry is an early, deliberate narrative plant for their later relationship. Removing it means the film fails to establish the relational asymmetry that defines their dynamic across multiple books. The audience loses context for why Ginny matters to Harry's world.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Burrow kitchen, Ginny's first appearance
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 2-5: Ginny gives a small squeal and runs out, and Ron explains she never shuts up normally but is atypically shy around Harry specifically because she has been talking about him all summer. The shyness is contextualised as a crush-driven exception to her normally voluble personality.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny squeals and dashes back up the stairs identically to the book, but Ron's line is trimmed to 'Ginny. Been talking about you all summer. Dead annoying, really.' The nuance that she 'never shuts up normally' – establishing her as a confident, talkative person whose shyness is the anomaly – is lost. The film presents only the shy, squealing girl with no counterweight.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book carefully frames Ginny's shyness as situational, not characterological. Dropping Ron's qualifier ('You don't know how weird it is for her to be this shy – she never shuts up normally') means the film audience's first and lasting impression is of a timid, starstruck girl rather than a confident one temporarily overwhelmed by a crush. This seeds a distorted baseline for the rest of her portrayal.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Flourish and Blotts, Ginny defends Harry against Draco
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 31: 'Leave him alone, he didn't want all that!' said Ginny. The narration notes this is the first time she had spoken in front of Harry, and she is described as glaring at Malfoy – a moment of courage that breaks her paralysing shyness.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film includes the line and the confrontation (Film Scene 1, Flourish and Blotts section), which is faithful. No damage here.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Faithful – not scored.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – King's Cross, Ginny goes through barrier
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 60: Mrs Weasley grabs Ginny's hand and they go through the barrier together, with no particular emphasis on Ginny being nervous. The scene is brief and functional.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film gives Ginny a small character beat: she looks 'a bit nervous', closes her eyes and slides through on her own while Mrs Weasley watches. While minor, the film chooses to emphasise nervousness as her defining state even in a routine action.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A small additional moment of portrayed nervousness that reinforces the 'timid Ginny' characterisation the film is building, with no book basis. Low weight because the moment is brief and isolated.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Howler scene, Ginny scribbling in the diary
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 68-78: Ginny is described as 'looking pale' around October; she is disturbed by Mrs Norris's fate (Scene 70), her lip trembles at Ron's dark jokes (Scene 71), and she is distraught in Charms (Scene 75). The book conveys emotional disturbance gradually across multiple scenes. Crucially, the book does not show Ginny writing in the diary in public view at the Gryffindor table during the Howler scene.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Immediately after the Howler, the film script notes: 'Ginny, sitting a bit apart from the others, looks up shyly, then returns to the SMALL BLACK BOOK she's scribbling in.' This is the film's first visual of Ginny with the diary, placed in a public, observable moment where Harry and Ron could in principle notice it.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book presents Ginny's possession of the diary as hidden and private – a source of secret shame by the end of the year. Showing her writing in it openly at the Gryffindor table undermines the sense that she is covertly controlled and struggling in private. It also slightly weakens the eventual revelation of the diary's significance, because the audience has already been flagged to associate the black book with Ginny long before Harry's investigation. The mystery and Ginny's hidden victimhood are both somewhat diluted.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Dueling Club, Ginny bolts from the room after Harry speaks Parseltongue
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 65-66 (context): After the dueling incident, the book describes students reacting with fear and suspicion toward Harry. Ron and Hermione discuss this with Harry. Ginny's specific reaction at the Dueling Club is not described in the provided book corpus beyond the general school atmosphere.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film script explicitly states: 'Malfoy looks shocked. Seamus and Neville's eyes glitter with fear. Ginny bolts the room.' This gives Ginny a uniquely fearful, flight reaction to Harry's Parseltongue – more extreme than any other named character.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While Ginny's fear in this moment has a diegetic explanation (she knows she is the one being controlled and fears discovery), the film presents it with no such subtext visible to the audience. The result is that Ginny is coded as simply terrified of Harry, reinforcing her one-dimensional fearful/shy portrayal and damaging the sense that she has a complex inner life. It also weakens the Harry–Ginny relationship by making her visibly flee him.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Library corridor, Ginny reacts to diary
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 83-85 (diary corridor scene): Ginny is described as staring from the diary to Harry 'looking terrified' when Malfoy picks up what he thinks is Harry's diary. This is a reaction the book attributes to her knowing the diary is Riddle's and fearing exposure.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 94 (corridor after Myrtle's bathroom): Harry jokes about his eyes being burned out by the diary; 'At the end of corridor, Ginny stands, looking from the diary to Harry – utter terror on her face – then dashes off. Harry: Ginny! I was only joking.' Ron says: 'Brilliant. Even your sister thinks I'm the monster now.'
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film frames Ginny's terror at the diary as if she fears Harry (played for a dark-comedy beat), and Harry himself interprets it as her believing he is dangerous. The book's equivalent moment is fear of exposure rooted in her guilt and Riddle's hold over her. The film's version erases Ginny's interiority and replaces it with a gag that makes her look simply credulous and fearful of Harry, further flattening her character.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Staircase / Quidditch corridor, Ginny spotted before match
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus does not contain this specific staircase scene. The provided book corpus shows Ginny's deterioration through scattered glimpses (pale, distraught, nightmares), but no equivalent staircase encounter before the Quidditch match.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 105A: 'Ron spies Ginny. Ron: Hey, Ginny! Going to the match? Ginny looks up, startled, then shakes her head and exits. Ron: I tell you, she gets weirder and weirder by the day...'
damaging_scenes.explanation: A brief added moment that reinforces 'weird/absent Ginny' as a recurring visual motif but gives her no interiority. Ron's dismissive commentary ('weirder and weirder') defines her distress entirely through another character's exasperated gaze, with no indication of her suffering. Minor in isolation but cumulative with other instances.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 – Chamber of Secrets, Ginny's awakening and dialogue
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 167-171: Ginny stirs, her eyes travel from the basilisk to Harry in his blood-soaked robes to the diary, she draws a shuddering gasp, and tears pour down her face. Her first words are: 'Harry -- oh, Harry -- I tried to tell you at b-breakfast, but I c-couldn't say it in front of Percy -- it was me, Harry -- but I -- I s-swear I d-didn't mean to -- R-Riddle made me, he t-took me over -- and - how did you kill that -- that thing? W-where's Riddle? The last thing I r-remember is him coming out of the diary --' She then weeps that she is going to be expelled, that she has looked forward to Hogwarts ever since Bill came, and fears what her Mum and Dad will say.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 133B/134: Ginny stirs, sees Harry, sobs: 'Harry. It was me! But I swear, I didn't mean to... Riddle made me. He wrote to me... took me over... I didn't even know whose diary it was. I found it inside my cauldron. The day we all went to Diagon Alley and... Harry. You're hurt...' In the tunnel (Scene 134): 'I'm going to be expelled, I just know it!'
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film removes Ginny's most emotionally resonant book line: her anguished statement that she tried to warn Harry at breakfast but couldn't say it in front of Percy. This is crucial – it establishes that Ginny had sufficient self-awareness and moral courage to attempt to confess before the crisis peaked, and it pays off the earlier breakfast scene (Book Scene 91-104) where she nearly told Harry and Ron. The film replaces this with a simpler denial of culpability. The loss removes her agency, her courage, and the emotional payoff of that earlier near-confession. Her fear about her parents and Hogwarts is retained but decontextualised from the deeper anguish the book conveys.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 – Dumbledore's office, Ginny's testimony and departure
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 198-211: Harry fears for Ginny's expulsion, worries how to protect her, and hesitates before telling the full story. Ginny herself sobs through her explanation ('His d-diary! I've b-been writing in it, and he's been w-writing back all year'). Mr Weasley is flabbergasted and scolds her. Dumbledore interrupts firmly to protect her and sends her to the hospital wing with kindness. The scene shows Ginny's guilt, vulnerability, parental reaction, and Dumbledore's protective wisdom all in sequence.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 135: Ginny repeats the cauldron explanation, adds 'But I understand if... given all the trouble I've caused... if you --' before Dumbledore cuts her off. Mr Weasley's scolding is relocated to the corridor (heard off-screen as Mrs Weasley's voice: 'A diary that writes back to you! Honestly, Ginny! What were you thinking? Haven't I always told you?'). The on-screen confrontation between Ginny and her father, and Ginny's extended tearful confession, are removed.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's resolution scene is one of the few moments where Ginny is given extended emotional space and where her relationship with her parents is developed. Mr Weasley's flabbergasted, loving-but-shaken response and Dumbledore's protective interruption form a complete emotional beat. The film reduces this to a brief appearance and relocates the parental reaction off-screen as a background gag (Mrs Weasley's scolding voice used for comedy). Ginny's emotional arc of guilt, relief, and parental reconnection is nearly entirely lost.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film – Absence of book's near-confession breakfast scene (Book Scenes 91-104)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 91-104: Ginny sits down next to Ron, looking tense, hands twisting in her lap. She is clearly trying to tell Harry and Ron something about the Chamber. She 'drew a deep breath' to speak, but Percy arrives and she 'jumped up as though her chair had just been electrified' and scampered away. This scene establishes Ginny as someone actively fighting Riddle's control and trying to do the right thing, at personal cost.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent scene exists in the film corpus. The film has no scene where Ginny attempts to warn Harry before the final crisis.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the single most damaging absence in the film's portrayal of Ginny. The near-confession is the clearest demonstration that Ginny has moral agency, courage, and is actively resisting Riddle's influence – she is not a passive victim but someone fighting back. Its absence means the film Ginny never attempts to save herself or others, never demonstrates internal resistance to the possession, and her awakening scene's reference to having tried to warn Harry (which the film also cuts) has no setup. The result is a Ginny who appears wholly passive throughout the plot, functioning only as a victim-object to be rescued rather than a character with her own moral struggle.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film – Absence of Ginny's active voice and humour in book's final train scene (Book Scenes 220-225)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 220-225: On the Hogwarts Express home, Ginny is 'perfectly happy again' and part of the group playing Exploding Snap and setting off fireworks. When Harry asks what she saw Percy doing, she giggles and reveals his secret girlfriend with obvious delight and mischief, showing her as warm, funny, and fully recovered – her authentic personality finally on display.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent scene in the film corpus. The film ends at the Great Hall feast and Dumbledore's office resolution. The train-home scene with Ginny's humour and recovery is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's closing Ginny moment is essential to her arc: it shows the real Ginny – confident, giggling, mischievous, fully herself – finally visible after a year of suppression. The film never delivers this resolution. The audience's last substantive impression of Ginny is the sobbing, frightened girl in the Chamber and Dumbledore's office. Her recovery, her personality, and the narrative promise that the 'real Ginny' exists beyond shyness and victimhood are never fulfilled on screen.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Leaky Cauldron) - Ginny's only line is a quip about Fred's nose
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 5 establishes that Ginny, though embarrassed around Harry, is a present and emotionally legible character in the Leaky Cauldron gathering. Book Scene 8 shows her giggling at Fred and George's irreverence. Book Scene 22 shows her sharing a knowing, conspiratorial look with Harry about Percy — a moment of genuine connection and shared humor between them.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny's sole contribution in the Leaky Cauldron sequence is a single throwaway line correcting Fred about whose nose looks big in the photo ('That's your nose, Fred'). The book's shy-but-present Ginny, who shares a laughing moment with Harry and registers emotionally to his presence, is replaced by a functional extra who delivers one comic beat and disappears.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses the Leaky Cauldron scenes to establish Ginny's embarrassed warmth toward Harry and a nascent sense of shared humor between them (the Percy moment). The film reduces her to a single gag line, erasing both her emotional reaction to Harry and the first seed of their personal connection. This quietly damages the relational groundwork the books lay early.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (Gryffindor corridor) - Ginny delivers the Fat Lady news with no emotional texture
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 33 shows Ginny visibly traumatized by the Dementor encounter on the train — shaking, huddled, needing comfort — establishing her as someone with a particular sensitivity to darkness (rooted in her possession by Voldemort in book 2). Book Scene 39 shows her making Harry a handmade get-well card, demonstrating initiative, care, and blushing courage despite her shyness.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny appears in the corridor scene purely as an information-delivery mechanism ('The Fat Lady... she's gone'). She has one further line ('No. You don't understand --') before the scene moves on. There is no interiority, no emotional register specific to her history with darkness and fear, and no characterization beyond plot function.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While delivering plot information is not inherently damaging, the film gives Ginny no distinguishing characterization in this moment. The book corpus establishes she has a heightened, history-specific response to fear and darkness. The film uses her as a neutral messenger, flattening a character who the books show is anything but neutral when it comes to encounters with evil.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 – Yule Ball dress robes scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book corpus, Ginny is not present in the dress robes scene. Her reaction to her own dress robes is not depicted. The film invents a line where Ginny dismisses her dress as 'ghastly,' which is a brief character moment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny says 'I'm not wearing that, it's ghastly' about her dress robes, then is immediately dismissed when Hermione clarifies the robes are for Ron. Ginny has no further presence or reaction.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The line is not damaging in itself — Ginny expressing a fashion opinion is consistent with book Scene 30 where she tells her mum she's old-fashioned. The moment is brief and isolated, causing minimal damage.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 – Yule Ball asking scene (Ginny comforting Ron)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus Scene 92–108 establishes Ginny as emotionally perceptive, warm but also wry and sharp. She sympathetically pats Ron's arm while 'fighting back a smile,' she defends Hermione ('She's not'), refuses to betray Hermione's secret ('I'm not telling you, it's her business'), and shows her own quiet dignity when revealing she's going with Neville — she 'looked extremely miserable' and bowed her head leaving, showing self-awareness and restrained emotion. She also shows moral backbone in not mocking Neville.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 4 shows Ginny saying 'It's all right, Ron. It's okay, Ron. It's all right. It doesn't matter' while comforting him, then serving mainly as a narrator of Ron's embarrassing Fleur encounter ('Actually, he sort of screamed at her. It was a bit frightening'). She functions as a reactive background figure and comic feed rather than displaying the book's mix of warmth, wit, self-restraint, and quiet dignity.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film strips Ginny's comforting to generic reassurance and reduces her to a punchline deliverer about Ron's screaming. Gone is her perceptiveness about Hermione's secret date, her refusal to gossip, her own emotional dignity about the Neville situation. She loses voice and complexity in favour of comic utility.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 – Ginny's Neville/Yule Ball situation entirely absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus Scene 108 is a significant characterisation beat: Ginny goes scarlet revealing she's going with Neville, explains she'd have no way to attend otherwise as a third-year, looks 'extremely miserable,' and leaves with her head bowed. This shows her vulnerability, her crush on Harry still present, and her dignity in an awkward situation. It also shows she was kind enough to say yes to Neville when Hermione turned him down.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Ginny and Neville arriving at the Yule Ball together (Film Scene 5) with no prior scene establishing how or why. The emotional beat — Ginny's embarrassed revelation, her misery, her kindness to Neville — is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The absence removes a defining moment that shows Ginny's emotional complexity (lingering feelings for Harry, wounded pride, kindness to Neville). Her Yule Ball appearance in the film is purely visual with no emotional grounding, making her seem like a background extra rather than a character with feelings at stake.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 – Yule Ball dancing (Ginny and Neville)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus Scene 109 establishes Ginny and Neville dancing nearby Harry, with Ginny wincing as Neville treads on her feet — a small but characterful detail showing her good-natured endurance and the slightly comic nature of the pairing, while she remains present in Harry's field of awareness.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 5 briefly shows Ginny and Neville entering and dancing, but the specific detail of Ginny wincing at Neville's clumsiness is absent. More significantly, Ginny is a visual background element only — she has no lines, no reaction shots, and no presence in the dramatic core of the scene, which focuses entirely on Harry, Ron, Hermione, and their dates.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor loss — the wincing detail is small, but its absence continues the pattern of flattening Ginny into a silent background figure throughout the Yule Ball sequence, compounding the damage from the missing pre-ball scene.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 – Yule Ball aftermath (Neville dancing with Ginny)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus does not place Ginny in a prominent role in the Yule Ball aftermath scene specifically, but has established her as a character with her own emotional stakes, voice, and reactions throughout the event.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 6 briefly shows 'Neville dancing with Ginny' in the Great Hall background while the emotional drama centres on Hermione crying on the stairs and Ron's jealousy. Ginny is purely decorative — a background visual with zero agency or dialogue.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Ginny's continued reduction to a silent background dancer through the entire Yule Ball sequence, combined with the missing emotional setup, means her characterisation across the entire Yule Ball arc is effectively erased. This entry captures the final compounding beat of that erasure.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 – Second task (Fred and George betting scene)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus Scene 112 shows Ginny as a comfortable social presence in the Harry/Weasley group, sitting with Fred, George, Harry, Hermione, and Ron at lunch, contributing to a warm group dynamic. She is a natural part of the inner circle.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 7 shows Fred and George running bets at the second task. Ginny appears briefly to say 'Don't be so mean' to Fred and George about their betting on the champions' survival. This is her only line in the entire second task sequence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The single line 'Don't be so mean' is broadly consistent with Ginny's character (she has moral instincts) and is not damaging in itself. It does, however, illustrate how thoroughly her role has been reduced to single-line reactions throughout the film. Low individual damage but symptomatic of the overall pattern.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – World Cup arrival (Ginny as silent background figure)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book corpus Scenes 47 establishes Ginny as observant and knowledgeable: she notes Bagman should know better than to talk about Bludgers near Muggles, showing she's attentive, understands Ministry security, and is willing to speak up with a pointed observation. She also laughs at Ron and Ginny's jokes (Scene 8), names Pigwidgeon (Scenes 17-18), and contributes to group conversation about Weasleys' Wizard Wheezes (Scenes 10, 13).
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: At the World Cup arrival in Film Scene 1, Ginny's only contribution is pointing at something and saying 'Look!' while Arthur says 'Keep up, girls' twice — grouping her with Hermione as charges to be managed. Her Bagman observation, her Pigwidgeon naming scene, her commentary on Fred and George's experiments — all are absent. She is visually present but characterologically silent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film establishes its version of Ginny in the World Cup sequence as a silent, reactive presence who says 'Look!' The book's Ginny is curious, perceptive, funny, and independently vocal. This early erasure sets the template for her treatment throughout the film and damages the audience's ability to understand who she is.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – DA meeting, Ginny casts Reducto during practice
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Ginny as a capable, confident, self-taught witch who secretly practiced Quidditch from age six and earned genuine respect. In DA lessons she performs very well: 'Ginny was teamed with Michael Corner; she was doing very well, whereas Michael was either very bad or unwilling to jinx her.' She is portrayed as naturally talented and poised.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny's only notable moment in DA practice is a single 'Reducto!' cast, shown briefly with no context, characterization, or indication of her standing out. She is visually present but given no personality, no banter, no interaction that conveys her skill, wit, or confidence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book carefully establishes Ginny as one of the DA's stronger performers, which seeds her later Quidditch role and her authority when she confronts Harry about possession. The film reduces her to a background extra in these scenes, erasing the foundation of her competence.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Hog's Head meeting, Ginny vouches for Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book Ginny says 'It's true' to support Harry's credentials, but this is embedded in a characterization where she is already known to the group as someone with her own standing — she is going out with Michael Corner, has recruited him and his friends, and is an active social agent in the DA's formation. Hermione notes 'Michael Corner and his friends wouldn't have come if he hadn't been going out with Ginny.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film Ginny says 'It's true' as one of several voices vouching for Harry, with no indication of her independent social network, her relationship with Michael Corner, or her role in recruiting members. Her agency in assembling the group is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book shows Ginny as a social actor with her own relationships and influence, not merely Harry's loyal hanger-on. Removing her recruitment role collapses her into a passive supporter and strips a key dimension of her independent characterization.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Umbridge's corridor, Ginny keeps watch with Garrotting Gas lie
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 322: Ginny spontaneously invents the Garrotting Gas cover story and explains its Fred-and-George origin, delivering it with convincing exasperation to skeptical students ('That's because it's colourless,' said Ginny in a convincingly exasperated voice, 'but if you want to walk through it, carry on, then we'll have your body as proof for the next idiot who doesn't believe us.'). This shows quick thinking, humor, and self-possession under pressure.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Ginny's role in the corridor watch is referenced only in passing ('Puking Pastilles, it wasn't pretty' — attributed to Ron for the diversion). The corridor watch scene itself is not depicted with Ginny's quick-witted improvisation; she simply appears afterward having escaped. Her inventive lie and the characterization it carries are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Garrotting Gas exchange is one of the book's most vivid demonstrations of Ginny's wit and composure under pressure. Its absence removes a clear, memorable beat that distinguishes her voice from the other characters.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Forest scene, Ginny absent from the group confronting Harry about Sirius
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 314–319: Ginny and Luna arrive together; Ginny says coolly 'There's no need to take that tone with me, I was only wondering whether I could help,' and immediately volunteers without hesitation ('Yeah, we'll do it'). She is assertive, unintimidated by Harry's frustration, and takes initiative.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, after escaping Umbridge's office Ginny appears with the group in the forest but has no lines or distinct characterization in this confrontation. The assertive, cool-headed exchange where she stands her ground against Harry's dismissiveness is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene establishes Ginny's emotional maturity and refusal to be condescended to by Harry — traits essential to her arc and to the eventual romantic dynamic. Without it, her presence in the rescue mission reads as passive inclusion rather than earned agency.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Forest scene, Ginny's argument for joining the rescue mission
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 357: Ginny argues fiercely for inclusion: 'I'm three years older than you were when you fought You-Know-Who over the Philosopher's Stone, and it's because of me that Malfoy's stuck back in Umbridge's office with giant flying bogies attacking him.' She names her own accomplishments directly, countering Harry's paternalism with logic and self-assertion.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny does not deliver this argument in the film. The group simply proceeds together without Ginny having to fight for her place or articulate her own competence and history.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of the most characterful moments Ginny has in the entire book — she asserts her own record and refuses to be dismissed. Its removal means the film audience never sees her advocate for herself, which is central to understanding her as an independent, strong-willed character rather than a background Weasley sibling.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 – Department of Mysteries battle, Ginny's Bat-Bogey Hex on Malfoy
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 349: Ron explicitly credits Ginny after the escape: 'Ginny was best, she got Malfoy — Bat-Bogey Hex — it was superb, his whole face was covered in the great flapping things.' This is her signature spell and a high-stakes combat achievement that earns peer recognition.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Ginny casting 'Reducto!' in the Hall of Prophecy battle, but the Bat-Bogey Hex on Malfoy — her signature, celebrated achievement in the escape from Umbridge's office — is not depicted or acknowledged. Her combat highlight is replaced with a generic spell shared by others.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Bat-Bogey Hex is Ginny's defining combat signature in the books and the basis for her later recognition by Slughorn. Its absence removes a memorable, character-specific moment and replaces it with an anonymous action.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 – Post-escape scene, Ginny missing from confrontation about possession
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 220–228: Ginny's most important scene in OotP. She confronts Harry's self-isolation about potential possession, draws on her own experience with Voldemort ('Well, that was a bit stupid of you, seeing as you don't know anyone but me who's been possessed by You-Know-Who, and I can tell you how it feels'), and definitively reassures him by diagnosing the difference between his experience and hers. This is emotionally central: she is the only person who can speak with authority here, and she does so with cool self-possession ('Lucky you,' said Ginny coolly).
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not occur in the film corpus. Ginny has no equivalent conversation with Harry about possession. The reassurance Harry receives about not being possessed comes through Occlumency/Snape's lessons and Dumbledore's concern, but Ginny's unique, personal, authoritative comfort is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the single most damaging omission. The possession-reassurance scene is the culmination of Ginny's arc in OotP: it establishes her as Harry's equal in suffering, demonstrates her as the one person uniquely positioned to help him, and forms the emotional foundation for their eventual relationship. It also recontextualizes her Chamber of Secrets experience as meaningful rather than merely historical. Its complete absence means the film audience has no basis for understanding why Harry might see Ginny as a peer or romantic interest, and Harry's fear of possession is resolved through external plot mechanics rather than intimate human connection.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 – Grimmauld Place arrival, Ginny reduced to background presence
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 1–42: At Grimmauld Place, Ginny is active and distinct — she tests the Imperturbable Charm with Dungbombs, contributes to sibling discussions about Percy with emotional depth ('It's been awful,' said Ginny sadly), makes a noise 'like an angry cat' at Percy's insults, rages loudly at being sent to bed ('Mum, I want to hear!'), and is noted to be likely awake waiting for information (Fred's aside about the Flobberworm). She is a full participant with her own voice.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1 shows Ginny briefly saying 'Hi, mum!' and being present at the dinner table/meeting area, but none of her active, characterful behavior from the book is depicted. Her testing of the charm, her emotional reactions to Percy, her protest at exclusion, and her defiant storming off are all absent. She is a visual background presence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Grimmauld Place is where the audience's first sustained impression of Ginny is formed. The book provides multiple distinct beats showing her intelligence, emotional range, and family loyalty. The film offers nothing beyond her face in the crowd, setting a pattern of erasure that persists throughout.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Library/Easter egg scene entirely absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 286–305: Ginny seeks Harry out privately in the library, delivers the Easter egg from Mrs. Weasley, notices his emotional state, listens carefully, and says: 'The thing about growing up with Fred and George is that you sort of start thinking anything's possible if you've got enough nerve.' She then helps devise the plan to reach Sirius via the fire. This is a one-on-one scene of warmth, perceptiveness, and practical courage.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No equivalent scene exists in the film corpus. The plan to contact Sirius via Umbridge's fireplace is developed differently, with no private Ginny-Harry moment, no Easter egg, and none of Ginny's perceptive attentiveness to Harry's emotional state.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is one of two key building blocks (alongside the possession scene) for the Harry-Ginny relationship. It shows Ginny as someone who seeks Harry out, reads him accurately, and offers both emotional warmth and practical help — not as Ron's sister but as her own person. Its absence means the film never shows them having a private, meaningful exchange, making any future romantic development narratively ungrounded.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 – Quidditch, Ginny as Seeker entirely absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 274–283: Ginny plays as Seeker in Harry's absence, catches the Snitch against Hufflepuff despite difficult conditions, is assessed by Harry with genuine admiration, and has an exchange with Harry where she corrects him about his ban ('You're banned as long as Umbridge is in the school. There's a difference.') and discusses Ron's situation with perceptive care. George also establishes her secret self-taught skill history.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: No Quidditch scenes involving Ginny appear in the film corpus. Her role as the team's Seeker, her performance under pressure, and the one-on-one conversation with Harry in the common room afterward are entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Ginny's Quidditch subplot establishes her as genuinely gifted and self-reliant, not merely a legacy Weasley. The common room scene after the match is a quiet but important moment of peer connection with Harry. Both the competence demonstration and the relationship-building beat are lost.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Scene 19-20 - Burrow attack / chase through reeds
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: No such attack on the Burrow occurs in HBP. Ginny's combat role in the book is limited to the school battle at the end of the novel (Book Scene 338), where she fights Amycus inside Hogwarts. The Burrow is a place of safety and domestic warmth in the book's summer section.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: An entirely invented sequence has Bellatrix and Greyback attack the Burrow at Christmas. Ginny races into the burning reeds against her father's orders, fights alongside Harry, and the two jointly blast Greyback. The scene ends with Harry and Ginny staring at each other wordlessly in the aftermath.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film manufactures a shared-danger romantic bonding moment between Harry and Ginny that has no book basis. In the books their relationship develops slowly through proximity, Quidditch, jealousy, and internal monologue over the entire year. By inventing a dramatic action set-piece as the engine of romantic connection, the film replaces the book's earned, psychologically grounded attraction with a generic action-movie shorthand. It also misrepresents Ginny's characterisation: her disobedience here reads as impulsive rather than brave-and-deliberate, and the scene removes the domestic Burrow atmosphere the book uses to contrast with the wider war.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Scene 17 - Burrow second floor, Ginny in towel
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes no private late-night meeting between Harry and Ginny at the Burrow over Christmas. Their Christmas interactions are domestic and group-based (decorating, meals, family dynamics with Fleur, the Percy visit). Harry's growing feelings are rendered through internal monologue, not charged private encounters.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny materialises alone with Harry in an upstairs corridor at night, hair wet from washing, in a robe. The scene is staged with deliberate romantic charge: 'the air prickling with silence,' Ginny eyeing him 'knowingly,' before wishing him Happy Christmas and departing. This scene is marked in the non-theatrical exclusion list but its framing device (the atmospheric setup) bleeds into the adjacent attack scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This invented encounter frames Ginny as a knowing, romantically aware figure initiating charged moments with Harry, rather than the book's version where Harry is the one silently wrestling with feelings while Ginny behaves normally around him. It shifts agency in the romantic arc from Harry's gradual internal awakening to Ginny actively signalling. The exclusion notice confirms this scene does not reach the theatrical cut, so the characterisation it establishes is lost — but the attack scene that immediately follows still depends on this framing to do romantic work the book never intended at this stage.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Scenes 23-25 - Room of Requirement / hiding the book / kiss
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book Harry hides the Potions textbook alone in the Room of Requirement (Book Scene 115 area). The first kiss between Harry and Ginny occurs spontaneously in the Gryffindor common room after Gryffindor wins the Quidditch Cup (Book Scene 317-319): Ginny runs toward him with a 'hard, blazing look,' Harry kisses her without planning it, in front of fifty people, after a year of suppressed longing. The kiss is Harry's action, born of joy and accumulated feeling.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny leads Harry to the Room of Requirement, takes the book from him, asks him to close his eyes, then initiates the kiss herself, framing it as 'another secret of sorts — one of mine,' before disappearing. Harry is passive and dazed.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's first kiss is a climactic payoff: Harry acts, spontaneously, in public, after the emotional arc of an entire year. The film's version inverts agency (Ginny initiates), removes the public stakes, eliminates the Quidditch euphoria context, and replaces yearning with a scripted 'secret.' This fundamentally alters the romantic dynamic — Ginny becomes the pursuer and Harry the passive recipient — which contradicts the book's careful construction of Harry as the one fighting his feelings. It also relocates the kiss to a private, pre-arranged space, draining it of the impulsive, crowd-witnessed bravery that makes the book moment resonate.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Scene 8 - Great Hall arrival, Ginny dabs Harry's face
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the equivalent book scene (Book Scene 109-110), Hermione cleans Harry's face with 'Tergeo.' Ginny is present at the table but it is Hermione who administers care. Ginny's relationship with Harry at this early point in the term is warm but not specially intimate — she is dating Dean and their proximity is that of old family friends.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny picks up a damp napkin and begins dabbing Harry's bloody face herself, then feels 'suddenly awkward' and hands it back. The screenplay note reads: 'there is something oddly charged in the moment, a surprise to both of them.'
damaging_scenes.explanation: A small but telling substitution: the film transfers Hermione's practical care-giving to Ginny and codes it as a charged romantic beat very early in the film. In the book, Harry and Ginny's mutual attraction develops across the whole year; introducing 'charge' this early, and having Ginny rather than Hermione perform the action, compresses and distorts the arc. It also subtly sidelines Hermione's role as Harry's primary emotional anchor in the trio.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Scene 13 - Slughorn's supper, Ginny arrives red-eyed and flustered
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book (Book Scene 88-107), Ginny is already seated in Slughorn's compartment when Harry and Neville arrive; she 'grimaced at Harry and Neville from behind Slughorn's back' — composed, wry, unruffled. She was invited because Slughorn witnessed her Bat-Bogey Hex. She defends Harry and Neville against Zabini with sharp wit ('Yeah, Zabini, because you're so talented... at posing'). Her eyes are not red and she is not flustered.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny arrives late, eyes red and 'uncharacteristically flustered,' because she and Dean have been fighting. Hermione whispers to Harry: 'Look at her eyes. They've been fighting again. Her and Dean.' Harry stands as she reaches the table — 'the only one' — and Hermione notes this with amusement.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book Ginny is composed and confident in this scene, deployed to show her wit and social ease; being upset over a boyfriend would be entirely out of character for the girl who told Ron it was 'none of your business' and calmly managed five rumoured boyfriends. The film makes her first significant solo scene one of romantic vulnerability rather than sharp competence. Additionally the scene is reoriented to serve Harry's growing feelings (he stands for her, Hermione notes it) rather than to establish Ginny's independent presence. This trades her book characterisation — confident, funny, self-possessed — for a love-interest signalling function.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Scene 7 - Hogwarts Express aisle, Ginny and Dean
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book (Book Scene 81-85), Ginny is 'a little way along the corridor, chatting to some friends.' Harry taps her on the shoulder and asks if she wants to find a compartment; she brightly declines ('I said I'd meet Dean') and walks off. Harry feels 'a strange twinge of annoyance' and notes he had become 'used to her presence.' This establishes Ginny as socially independent, popular, and at ease — Harry's feelings register as an intrusion into his own consciousness.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny is shown in the aisle with Dean whispering to her, while she looks 'more interested in the purple Pygmy Puff perched on her shoulder' than in Dean. She receives Luna with mild politeness. There is no interaction with Harry.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A minor but symptomatic loss: the book's train corridor beat efficiently establishes Ginny's independence, Harry's nascent jealousy, and the social dynamic between them at the start of term. The film omits the Harry-Ginny exchange entirely, removing an early marker of Harry's suppressed feelings and Ginny's easy self-sufficiency. Low impact on its own but part of a pattern of stripping the slow-burn arc.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Scene 16 - Burrow Christmas dinner, tart scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's Christmas at the Burrow (Book Scenes 206-218) features Ginny as one voice among many — teasing Fred and George, decorating lavishly, playing Exploding Snap, comforting Mrs. Weasley, and claiming credit for spattering Percy with parsnip. Her interactions with Harry are warm but unremarkable. There is no private food-sharing moment staged as a romantic beat.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: During the Christmas dinner, Ginny approaches Harry specifically, asks 'Don't trust me?' and pops a tart she made herself into his mouth. Ron immediately 'plops down between them' as self-appointed big-brother guardian.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The scene recasts Ginny as actively seeking out and feeding Harry in a deliberately intimate gesture, then plays Ron's interruption for romantic-comedy beats. In the book their Christmas dynamic is affectionate but embedded in the larger Weasley family scene; there is no staged intimacy. The film is again collapsing the slow-burn book arc into a series of manufactured romantic moments, and making Ginny the initiator in each one rather than Harry — inverting the book's careful distribution of agency.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Scene 22 - Hospital wing, Ginny whispers to Harry about Ron and Hermione
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book hospital wing scene (Book Scene 237-258), Ginny is one of several people present and participates actively in the group's analytical discussion about how Ron was poisoned — contributing real reasoning ('the poisoner could just as easily have been after Dumbledore,' Book Scene 254). She is a participant, not a romantic accessory.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny's only line in this film scene is a whispered aside to Harry about Ron and Hermione: ''Bout time, don't you think?' The screenplay notes Harry 'watches her go, hopelessly smitten.'
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film reduces Ginny's book role — active analytical contributor who reasons through the poisoning mystery — to a single line that functions only to (a) advance the Ron/Hermione subplot and (b) give Harry a reason to stare at her. Her intelligence and plot-relevant reasoning are cut entirely. This is consistent with the film's pattern of retaining Ginny only in scenes that serve the romantic arc.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film - Absence of Quidditch arc scenes (practice, match, Ginny as Seeker, post-match kiss)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 116-184 and 317-319 establish Ginny across an extended Quidditch arc: she earns her Chaser place on merit ('outflown all competition, scored seventeen goals'), shows sharp wit at Ron's expense during practice, crashes into Zacharias Smith's commentary box deliberately, and is the recipient of the book's climactic spontaneous first kiss after Gryffindor wins. These scenes collectively establish her athletic excellence, her humor, her integration into the team, and the specific joy-fuelled context of the real kiss.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film includes the tryouts montage (Ginny flies well) and a brief Quidditch match glimpse, but eliminates the extended practice scenes, the Zacharias commentary-box incident, and crucially replaces the post-match common-room kiss (Harry initiates, public, after Gryffindor win) with the private Room of Requirement kiss initiated by Ginny (Film Scenes 23-25).
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Quidditch arc is the primary vehicle through which Ginny's competence, humor, and independent personality are shown — not told. Her wit ('forgot to brake, Professor, sorry'), her performance, her integration into the team as an equal are all established here. The film's substitution of a private scripted kiss for the book's public spontaneous one is the single most structurally damaging change: it removes Harry's agency at the moment of culmination, eliminates the Quidditch triumph as emotional trigger, and loses Ginny's 'hard blazing look' which the book explicitly echoes at Dumbledore's funeral (Book Scene 402) — a thematic callback the film cannot make. The loss of this arc is the core reason why Ginny's film characterisation feels thin.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film - Absence of Harry/Ginny relationship scenes (Felix Felicis planning, walks by lake, 'Ron's permission' exchange)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 320-327 depict Harry and Ginny as an established couple: sitting together in the common room, Ginny making jokes about Romilda Vane's tattooed-Hippogriff rumours, the 'Ron's permission' exchange where Ginny sharply dismisses Ron's possessiveness ('Since when did you give me permission to do anything?'), Harry reflecting that he has 'never been happier.' These scenes show Ginny as funny, confident, romantically self-assured, and equal in the relationship.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: After the Room of Requirement kiss the film provides no scenes of Harry and Ginny as an actual couple. The film moves directly toward the climax. The 'Ron's permission' exchange is entirely absent. Ginny's wit, equality in the relationship, and self-assurance in this context are never shown.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Without the 'being together' scenes, the audience has no sense of what the Harry-Ginny relationship is — only that a kiss happened and Harry is 'smitten.' The book uses these scenes to cement Ginny as someone Harry is genuinely happy with and to show her personality at its most relaxed and funny. Their absence means the break-up at Dumbledore's funeral (Film Scene 28/30) carries almost no emotional weight because the film has not established what is being lost. This is an arc-level failure: the audience cannot mourn a relationship they have not witnessed.

damaging_scenes.scene: HBP Film Scenes 28/30 - Break-up at Dumbledore's funeral/Astronomy Tower aftermath
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book (Book Scenes 402-407), the break-up occurs at Dumbledore's lakeside funeral. Ginny does not cry. She meets Harry's gaze with 'the same hard, blazing look' as after the Quidditch win — 'and he knew that at that moment they understood each other perfectly.' She says: 'I never really gave up on you... I knew you wouldn't be happy unless you were hunting Voldemort. Maybe that's why I like you so much.' This is a fully articulated, emotionally mature exchange that shows Ginny's depth and her specific understanding of who Harry is.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has no equivalent break-up scene with meaningful dialogue. At the Astronomy Tower aftermath (Film Scene 28), Ginny steps forward and Harry leans his head on her shoulder while she strokes him. At the Astronomy Tower epilogue (Film Scene 30), Ginny and Ron stand 'just out of earshot' while Harry and Hermione discuss the future; Ginny has no lines. Hermione tells Harry 'Ron's okay with it, you know. You and Ginny. But if I were you, when he's around, I'd keep the snogging to a minimum.'
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's break-up scene is arguably Ginny's most important moment in the entire novel: it demonstrates her emotional intelligence, self-knowledge, and mature acceptance without self-pity — qualities that define her as a character rather than merely a love interest. The film eliminates this entirely. Ginny is reduced to a comforting physical presence after Dumbledore's death and then a silent figure in the epilogue. The thematic resonance of her 'hard blazing look' — connecting the Quidditch kiss to the funeral farewell — is made impossible by the film's restructuring. This is the most structurally damaging single omission: it collapses Ginny from a character with interiority and arc into a background romantic prop at the story's emotional climax.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (INT. KITCHEN - MORNING): Ginny zipping scene / birthday kiss
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes that Harry's 17th birthday kiss happens in Ginny's bedroom, initiated by Ginny with deliberate emotional weight: she gives him a present, speaks with quiet wit about veela and 'dating opportunities,' then kisses him 'as she had never kissed him before.' It is a private, emotionally loaded moment. Ginny is 'rarely weepy,' composed, and the scene ends with her showing emotional strength even as Harry feels he must pull away. The interrupted kiss is followed by Ginny turning her back, possibly suppressing tears — the whole sequence is rich with unspoken feeling and Ginny's dignity.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film replaces the book's emotionally resonant birthday scene with a sensualised 'zip me up' encounter — Ginny in a low-cut dress, back exposed, Harry's fingers lingering on her skin — followed by a lingering kiss that George interrupts. The intimate setup is constructed around physical suggestion rather than Ginny's wit, agency, or emotional composure. The book's Ginny initiates with a gift, a joke, and a deliberate choice; the film's Ginny is more passive object of a charged heterosexual tableau. Her voice and personality are largely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The birthday scene is one of Ginny's most characterised moments in the books — it shows her composure, humour, and emotional intelligence. Replacing it with a physical/sensual scene strips her of the very traits that make her romantic relationship with Harry credible and earned. Audience understanding of why Harry loves her (her strength, wit, and self-possession) is weakened in favour of visual aesthetics.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (INT. KITCHEN - MORNING): Ginny's dialogue about the mission
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Harry and Ginny have a charged private conversation while laying the table, where Ginny perceptively explains her mother's blocking strategy and Harry accidentally reveals the truth about Voldemort. When Ginny presses 'So it's true? That's what you're trying to do?', Harry is evasive. Ginny stares at him with 'something more than shock' — she is processing real danger, not asking for reassurance. The scene shows her intelligence and emotional perceptiveness.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses Ginny's dialogue to a brief, functional exchange about Dumbledore's secrecy, with her asking 'And Ron and Hermione — they'll not be going back to Hogwarts either?' before pivoting to the zip scene. She accepts Harry's non-answer with 'I see' and moves on. The book's demonstration of her deductive intelligence and the emotional weight of realising Harry is walking toward death are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene shows Ginny piecing together dangerous truths and reacting with genuine emotional complexity. The film reduces her to a compliant recipient of a one-line justification. Her intelligence and perceptiveness — key traits — are lost, making her feel like a passive love interest rather than an active, understanding partner.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (EXT. THE BURROW - NIGHT): Ginny's reaction to George's injury
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, when George is brought in, Ginny gasps at the sight of the wound and is actively described tending to George alongside Mrs. Weasley. She answers Harry's unspoken plea for information about the missing Order members. She is practical, informative, and emotionally present without being hysterical — she gives Harry the status update on portkeys and who is still missing.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Ginny cry 'Oh my God! George!' with hands flying to her face — a brief reactive beat — and she has no subsequent role tending to him. Her practical, informative function (the portkey briefing) is retained as a brief line but the scene of her and Mrs. Weasley actively tending George together is absent. Her reaction is purely emotional rather than a combination of emotion and capable action.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but consistent: the book shows Ginny as someone who acts under pressure rather than just reacting. The hands-to-face gasp is a stereotypically feminine shock response; the book's Ginny moves straight into practical tending. Isolated, this is low damage, but it contributes to a cumulative pattern of reducing her competence.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (EXT. THE BURROW): Ginny takes Harry's hand in the vigil
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 23 explicitly describes: 'As they walked down the back steps into the dark yard, Ginny took his hand.' This is Ginny's initiative — a quiet, wordless act of comfort and connection at a moment of shared dread. Book Scene 18 also shows Ginny and Harry sharing a look, Harry wanting to hold her, restrained only by Mrs. Weasley's presence. The vigil scene (Scenes 23-25) establishes Ginny as emotionally attuned and quietly brave, standing the silent watch with Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film does not include the hand-holding during the vigil in the yard. Ginny is present in the Burrow scenes and gives the portkey briefing, but the intimate moment of her taking Harry's hand — and the extended silent vigil — is not present in the film corpus. The emotional bonding during the wait for the missing Order members is largely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This quiet moment of Ginny taking Harry's hand is one of the book's clearest signals that their relationship is real and mutual even under crisis. Its absence means the film's Harry-Ginny connection relies almost entirely on the 'zip' scene rather than demonstrated emotional partnership. The relationship feels less grounded.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 8 (INT. HOGWARTS EXPRESS): Ginny's brief appearance
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes (Scene 143) that Ginny had been banned from Hogsmeade and was leading ongoing DA resistance at Hogwarts under Snape's regime — a brave, ongoing act of defiance. Scene 120 shows Harry imagining Ginny, Neville, and Luna sitting together on the train 'debating how best to undermine Snape's new regime.' Ginny is shown as an active leader of resistance throughout Harry's absence.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Ginny briefly in a train compartment, passive, sitting among other students as Dark Wizards search the train. She does not speak or act. Neville bars the searchers' way. Ginny's established role as a resistance leader at Hogwarts is entirely invisible in this scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film reduces one of the few glimpses of Ginny's Hogwarts resistance to a silent background presence, with Neville taking the visible defiant action. Given that Ginny's resistance leadership is a significant part of her arc in the book during Harry's absence — and one of the things that makes her his equal — this erasure damages audience understanding of who she is during this period.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 11 (INT. ROOM OF REQUIREMENT): Ginny's arrival / Ron's comment
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 169 describes Ginny climbing through the hole and giving Harry 'a radiant smile.' Harry 'had forgotten, he had never fully appreciated, how beautiful she was, but he had never been less pleased to see her' — because he fears for her safety. This is a complex, bittersweet moment that conveys the depth and cost of his love. The book also establishes (Scene 163) that Ginny led DA resistance until Easter, when she 'never came back after Easter' — implying she was removed from Hogwarts for her activities.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Ginny appear with the functional line 'Snape knows. He knows that Harry was spotted in Hogsmeade.' Ron comments 'Six months she hasn't seen me and it's like I'm Frankie First Year. I mean, I'm only her brother.' Her arrival is played partly for comedic sibling dynamic. Harry's complex internal response — the painful beauty of seeing her — is absent, as is any reference to her resistance activities being the reason she's here.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Ginny arrival is one of the saga's most quietly devastating beats about what Harry has sacrificed. The film flattens it to a functional information-delivery entrance with a comedy beat from Ron. Harry's interior recognition of what she means to him — and costs him — is entirely lost, weakening the emotional stakes of the Harry-Ginny relationship at a critical moment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 12 (INT. MARBLE STAIRCASE): Hand-holding under Invisibility Cloak
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not feature this specific Cloak hand-holding beat in the staircase. However, this is a film addition rather than a removal, so it is not inherently damaging. Assessed for faithfulness: the gesture is consistent with book characterisation of Ginny knowing Harry's touch. This scene is largely neutral to faithful.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film adds a brief tender moment of Harry reaching out to hold Ginny's hand as he moves invisibly through the crowd. She 'doesn't look back, knows it's him, knows his touch.' This is a film invention but tonally consistent with the book's established intimacy.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This addition is gentle and consistent with book characterisation. It does not cause damage — if anything it briefly serves the relationship. Not a damaging entry; included only to note it was assessed and found neutral/positive.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 13 (INT. GREAT HALL): Ginny steps in front of Harry when Pansy points
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not have a direct equivalent of this specific beat in the provided corpus. However, Ginny's protective instinct and DA loyalty are thoroughly established in the book. This is a film addition.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Ginny instinctively steps in front of Harry, wand drawn, when Pansy Parkinson calls for someone to grab him. This is a characterisation-consistent addition that shows Ginny's loyalty and courage in a visible, active way.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is a faithful addition that reinforces Ginny's courage. Not damaging. Included to confirm it was assessed.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scenes 14-18 (EXT. WOODEN BRIDGE): Ginny's role in the bridge sequence
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book (Scene 169, 178-192) places Ginny in the Room of Requirement during the battle, actively trying to fight, being physically restrained by Mrs. Weasley, arguing for her right to be in the battle. She is eventually permitted to stay in the Room of Requirement. The book shows her at a window sending 'a well-aimed jinx into a crowd of fighters below' (Scene 206) and comforting Tonks (Scene 209). Her battle role is distributed across the castle. The book does not feature a bridge demolition subplot involving Ginny.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film creates a substantial original action sequence where Ginny, Neville, and Seamus demolish the wooden bridge to stop Snatchers. Ginny is shown as competent and brave in this sequence, stands ready with her wand, steadies Neville, and participates actively in the battle.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is an invention that actually gives Ginny visible active agency, which partially compensates for the removal of her book battle moments. The damage is not from what is added here, but from what is absent: her confrontation with Mrs. Weasley, her fight to stay and be part of the battle, and her jinxing fighters from a window — all of which show her fighting spirit against her family's protectiveness. The invented sequence gives her action but removes her emotional arc of arguing for her own right to fight. Net damage is low.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 19 (INT. MARBLE STAIRCASE): Ginny-Harry moment mid-battle ('I know. Then she is off.')
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book (Scenes 206-211) has Ginny and Harry exchange urgent words during battle — Harry telling her to keep safe, Ginny fighting beside Tonks and comforting her. The relationship is present but framed around duty and danger. Harry's interior state — his terror of losing her — is shown through narration (Scene 215: 'he wanted to find the other Weasleys, and above all make sure, make quite sure, that Ginny was not — but he could not permit that idea to form in his mind'). Scene 232 has Harry, about to be killed by Voldemort, thinking inexplicably of 'Ginny, and her blazing look, and the feel of her lips on his.'
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film compresses the Harry-Ginny mid-battle connection to a single exchange: their eyes meet, Ginny says 'I know,' then runs. It is intimate and efficient but strips the texture of their shared danger, Harry's terror for her, and the extended moments they spend in proximity during the battle.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The 'I know' moment is elegant cinema but it replaces a richer battle-time dynamic. Most significantly, Harry's private terror of losing Ginny — one of the book's most powerful articulations of why she matters to him — is unrepresented in the film. His thought of her in his final walk to death (Scene 232) has no film equivalent in this corpus, meaning the emotional through-line of Ginny as what Harry has to lose is not adequately conveyed.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 21 (EXT. HOGWARTS GROUNDS): Ginny comforting injured girl while Harry passes invisibly
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 221-228 show Harry, under the Cloak walking to his death, stopping when he sees Ginny crouching over an injured girl, whispering 'It's all right. It's ok. We're going to get you inside.' Ginny's voice breaks. Harry 'wanted to shout out to the night, he wanted Ginny to know that he was there... He wanted to be stopped, to be dragged back.' He forces himself to walk on. This is one of the book's most emotionally devastating passages — Ginny as the embodiment of everything Harry is sacrificing.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film includes this scene with reasonable fidelity: Ginny says 'It's all right. We're going to get you inside' and 'Don't worry. I won't leave you. I promise.' The film adds 'I kept calling. No one came' for the girl. Ginny is shown as 'haunted by sorrow.' Harry studies her, moved, then continues. The film omits Harry's interior anguish ('he wanted Ginny to know he was there... he wanted to be stopped') but the visual of him watching her is present.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The scene is present and reasonably faithful in action, but Harry's devastating interior monologue — which makes Ginny the emotional anchor of his sacrifice — is necessarily absent in film form and not compensated for by visual storytelling. The weight of the moment is reduced. Some damage, but the scene itself is not unfaithful in portrayal of Ginny specifically.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 23 (EXT. COURTYARD): Ginny's reaction to Harry's apparent death
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 235 describes Ron's, Hermione's, and Ginny's voices crying out 'Harry! HARRY!' as he lies still — the worst thing Harry has to endure in that moment. Scene 234 and 235 establish that Ginny is one of the three voices he hears, alongside Ron and Hermione. The book does not include Ginny charging toward Voldemort, but her grief is articulated as a voice Harry can hear.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film has Ginny cry 'No... NO!' and physically rush toward Voldemort, only stopped by Arthur. Voldemort then mocks her: 'Stupid girl. You cry for that?' This is a film invention — a visible, dramatic expression of grief. Ginny is singled out and publicly humiliated by Voldemort.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film replaces Ginny's book grief (a voice Harry hears, equally weighted with Ron and Hermione) with an impulsive physical rush at Voldemort that results in her being publicly mocked and restrained. This repositions her from a figure of equal emotional weight alongside the trio to a visually dramatic but narratively passive figure who must be physically stopped by her father. The 'stupid girl' taunt from Voldemort, while dramatically effective, reduces her to spectacle. Her grief is individualised in a way the book avoids — the book is careful not to make Harry's death primarily about romantic loss.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 25 (INT. GREAT HALL - AFTERMATH): Ginny's role in the epilogue of the battle
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 239 shows Harry walking through the Great Hall after the battle. He spots Ginny 'two tables away; she was sitting with her head on her mother's shoulder: There would be time to talk later, hours and days and maybe years in which to talk.' This is a quiet, forward-looking moment — Harry seeing her and knowing the future is open. The book's epilogue (Scenes 241-277) gives Ginny substantial presence as a confident, warm, actively parenting equal partner — she speaks frequently, makes jokes ('You interrupted them? You are so like Ron'), manages the children, and Harry looks at her with love at the close.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 25 shows Ginny 'puffy-eyed and pale, standing alongside a distraught Arthur and Molly' — she is part of the family grief tableau. The film's epilogue (Scenes 26-27) shows an older Ginny who appears briefly, takes the trolley, and is present but largely silent compared to the book epilogue where she has multiple warm, funny, and characterised lines.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book epilogue is one of the few places the adaptation had to show Ginny as Harry's genuine equal in adult life — warm, funny, and present. The film epilogue reduces her to a background parenting presence. Several of her best lines (teasing James about interrupting Teddy, writing to James three times a week, the Albus Severus moment) are compressed or cut, meaning the lasting impression of Ginny as Harry's wife is thinner than the books intend.

damaging_scenes.scene: Structural absence across DH Part 1: Ginny's Hogwarts resistance arc is entirely absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes across multiple scenes (120, 123, 127-137, 141, 143-144, 153, 163) that Ginny is a central figure in the Hogwarts resistance during Harry's absence: she leads DA activities, is punished, is banned from Hogsmeade, and is eventually removed from school. Harry tracks her on the Marauder's Map, stares at her name, and the scant news of her resistance makes him 'want to see her so badly it felt like a stomachache.' This arc establishes Ginny as doing something meaningful and brave while Harry is gone — she is not waiting passively.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In DH Part 1, Ginny has no presence whatsoever after leaving at the wedding. The film contains no indication of her resistance activities at Hogwarts, no reference to her being punished or removed, no Marauder's Map moment showing Harry thinking of her. She disappears from the film entirely until the Room of Requirement arrival in Part 2.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the most structurally significant damage. The book's Ginny has a parallel arc during Harry's absence that confirms she is not a passive love interest but an active agent of resistance. Its complete absence means the film's Ginny has no arc of her own during the central film of the trilogy. She exists only as a romantic object Harry misses, rather than a person doing important and dangerous things independently. This fundamentally weakens her as a character and, by extension, weakens the credibility of Harry's love for her — since the audience has no evidence of what she is doing or who she is when he's not present.
